question_text: Express 1 + i√3 in the modulus-amplitude form.

mark_split.label: Find the amplitude θ from the quadrant and write r(cos θ + i sin θ)

recall_prompt: Say how you would write a complex number in modulus-amplitude form — what two numbers you need and how the quadrant fixes the angle.
insider_note: The point (1, √3) is in the first quadrant, so θ = π/3 needs no adjustment — still write the quadrant sentence, because it is part of the second mark on every modulus-amplitude answer. Keep the r = 2 in front of the bracket.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find r
steps.margin_note: First mark. x = 1, y = √3, so r = √(1 + 3) = 2.
lines: Let 1 + i√3 = x + iy ⇒ x = 1, y = √3

recall.must_convey: That x = 1, y = √3 and the modulus r = √(1 + 3) = 2.
accept: x is one, y is root three, r is root of one plus three which is two
the modulus is root four equals two
r equals root x squared plus y squared, that is two
one plus three is four, root of that is two

steps.why: r is the distance from the origin and goes in front of the bracket. (√3)² = 3, not √3 — the square removes the root.

steps.label: Find θ and write the form
steps.margin_note: Second mark. tan θ = √3 and the point (1, √3) is in the first quadrant, so θ = π/3 with no adjustment.
steps.memory_tip: First quadrant, so the acute angle stands: θ = π/3 with no adjustment. Keep the r = 2 in front.
lines: (1, √3) lies in the first quadrant ⇒ θ = π/3

recall.must_convey: That tan θ = √3 with the point in the first quadrant gives θ = π/3, so the form is 2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3).
accept: tan theta is root three and the point is in the first quadrant so theta is pi by three
the modulus amplitude form is two times cos pi by three plus i sin pi by three
first quadrant, theta equals pi by three
point first quadrant lo undi kabatti theta pi by three
amplitude pi by three and modulus two

steps.why: In the first quadrant the amplitude is the acute angle itself, so tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3 is the answer with no correction. Writing the quadrant line anyway is good practice — it is the line that earns the mark in the other quadrants.
common_mistakes: Writing θ = 60° when the paper expects radians (both are accepted, but be consistent).
Forgetting the r = 2 in front of the bracket.
